parsed.hook: Tessellae Old Vines sits in the part of Côtes du Roussillon where old-vine Carignan and Grenache can turn sun into structure instead of jam. That matters here because the southern Roussillon gives you heat, but the tramontane wind and the area’s dry, stony soils keep the wine from collapsing into sweetness.
parsed.wine_summary:
Lafage is one of the clearest names in Roussillon for wines that trade on place rather than polish, and Tessellae Old Vines fits that lane. The wine comes from Côtes du Roussillon, an umbrella appellation where red wines can be built from Carignan, Grenache, Lledoner Pelut, Mourvèdre, and Syrah; even without the exact blend for this bottling, that framework tells you the wine is built for dark fruit, Mediterranean herb tones, and tannin shaped by heat and old-vine low yields.

What makes this wine matter is the combination of old vines and a region that naturally gives concentration. Old vines usually mean lower crop loads and smaller berries, so you get more skin-derived flavor, more grip, and less easy fruit. In market terms, that often makes Lafage a smart buy for drinkers who want southern French character without jumping to pricier Roussillon cru bottlings or to more expensive Languedoc bottlings with a similar sun-baked profile.
parsed.terroir_expression: Côtes du Roussillon sits on the southern edge of France near the Pyrenees, where the climate is hot, dry, and wind-scoured by the tramontane, a cold, powerful northwesterly that reduces disease pressure and preserves freshness. The soils across the appellation are mixed, but the classic components are schist, gneiss, limestone, and stony alluvial terraces; those rocky substrates drain fast and force roots deep, which is why these wines taste concentrated rather than bloated. In the glass, that usually means black cherry, blackberry, garrigue herbs, and a salty, rocky finish instead of sweet, ripe plum.
parsed.vinification_summary: Tessellae Old Vines is made to preserve the weight that old vines naturally give, while keeping the wine drinkable and not over-extracted. When a winemaker manages extraction carefully, it means they control how much color, tannin, and flavor are pulled from grape skins and seeds during fermentation; in a southern wine like this, that matters because too much extraction can turn ripe fruit into hard bitterness. The goal is usually a dry red with enough structure for food, but enough juiciness to keep the fruit moving.
parsed.food_pairing:
Confit de canard with crispy potatoes — the wine’s dark fruit and firm tannin cut through duck fat, while the savory herb notes echo the rendered skin.
Nashville hot chicken — the fruit cools the chile heat, and the tannin grabs the fried crust without making the spice feel harsher.
Lamb shawarma with tahini and pickled onions — the spice rub and char meet the wine’s Mediterranean herbal side, while the acidity in the wine handles the garlic and fat.
Porcini mushroom risotto — the earthy mushrooms line up with the wine’s rocky, savory edge, and the soft starch keeps the tannins from feeling blunt.
Cassoulet from Toulouse — this is the classic southern French pairing logic: beans, pork, duck, and slow-cooked richness need a red with grip, not perfume.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Domaine du Clos des Fées Côtes du Roussillon — similar southern Roussillon concentration, with the same sun-plus-stone profile and food-friendly tannin.
Château de Saint-Cosme Les Deux Albions — comparable for Rhône-adjacent black fruit, garrigue, and a dry, savory finish at a similar everyday-premium level.
M. Chapoutier Côtes du Roussillon Villages — another benchmark for structured southern French red with dark fruit and mineral grip.
parsed.style_profile: Old-vine Mediterranean red with medium-plus body, firm tannins, and savory, sun-baked depth
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink from now through the next 4 to 6 years, especially if the vintage is 2018 or 2014 and the bottle has been stored cool and dark. Keep it at cellar temperature and give older bottles some air; this style can tighten up after opening and usually improves over the first hour.
parsed.value_assessment: At the LCBO price point in Canadian dollars, this sits in the value-red category where Roussillon has a real advantage over many better-known French regions. It should compete with Côtes du Rhône bottlings from Guigal and E. Guigal Côtes du Rhône at the shelf level, and with similarly priced Languedoc reds from producers like Gérard Bertrand; I’d buy this if you want more structure and regional identity than generic southern French blend. The payoff is better concentration and a clearer sense of sun, stone, and old vines.
parsed.market_position: Restaurant buyers can use this as a by-the-glass or bottle-list southern French red for duck, lamb, and mushroom dishes because it has enough tannin for food without needing long decanting. On retail shelves, it belongs in the “serious everyday red” slot for drinkers who already buy Côtes du Rhône and want a step toward Roussillon’s stonier, darker profile without moving into collector pricing.
parsed.insider_take: The mistake is treating this like a soft, fruity Mediterranean quaffer. Old vines in Roussillon usually mean more grip, more savory depth, and less easy charm, so this is better for the drinker who wants dinner wine with backbone than for someone hunting plush fruit. Skip it if you want brightness and lift; buy it if you want a red that can handle braise, smoke, and spice without falling apart.
